title: The Future of Entrepreneurship Research Includes Online Panel Data—If Used Correctly
authors: Jeffrey M. Pollack; J. Jeffrey Gish; Timothy L. Michaelis; Jeni L. Burnette; David J. Scheaf; Jon C. Carr; Nicholas A. Smith
affiliations: Management, Innovation, and Entrepreneurship, NC State University, Raleigh, NC, USA; Whitman School of Management, Syracuse University, NY, USA; Department of Psychology, NC State University, Raleigh, NC, USA; Hankamer School of Business, Baylor University, Waco, TX, USA; Northern Illinois University, DeKalb, IL, USA
abstract: As online panel data (OPD) become more widely used across the behavioral sciences, editors, reviewers, and researchers in entrepreneurship are asking whether it has a legitimate place in our field. We believe the answer is yes—provided three conditions are met. First, the online panel’s participants and definition of entrepreneur must match the research question. Second, studies must incorporate best practices for sample verification. Third, generalizability must be explicitly addressed as part of the study (or set of studies). If researchers do these things, OPD can meaningfully advance both theory and practice in entrepreneurship research. That said, real questions remain. What kinds of studies are suitable for OPD? Who are these respondents, and are they who they say they are? Are they human, and are they entrepreneurs as commonly defined in the literature? Our recommendations and checklist aim to enable entrepreneurship researchers to answer these questions and make informed choices when collecting data and publishing results using OPD.

title: Dueling Political Fictions and Public Administration and Democracy in an Era of Populism and Authoritarian Impulses
authors: Michael W. Spicer
affiliations: Cleveland State University Cleveland Ohio USA
abstract: ABSTRACT The political fictions used in political discourse, during the English Civil War period, remain relevant to contemporary public policy and administration. Mainstream public administration discourse has too often employed the fiction of a singular and unbounded popular sovereignty that emerged during this period, leaving public administration ill‐equipped to deal with the authoritarian impulses of contemporary populist governments. What is needed in public administration discourse, in dealing with these authoritarian impulses, is not an ethic of administrative neutrality, such as has traditionally dominated much of our field, but an ethic of constitutionalism that draws on the fiction of the individual that was also articulated during the English Civil War period by the English Levellers and subsequently by the founders of the American Constitution.

Estimating the Pricing Kernel: A Simple Regression-Based Dimension-Reduction Approach
authors: Bin Luo; Guofu Zhou; Ti Zhou
affiliations: College of Business, Southern University of Science and Technology, Shenzhen 518055, China; Olin School of Business, Washington University in St. Louis, St. Louis, Missouri 63130; School of Economics and Management, Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen 518055, China
abstract: We propose a simple framework for estimating the pricing kernel in factor space by constructing the mean–variance efficient factor portfolio via an ordinary least squares formulation with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regularization. The method accommodates high-dimensional settings in which the number of candidate factors exceeds the sample size and automatically shrinks redundant factor weights toward zero. We show theoretically that the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of the estimated portfolio converges to the theoretical maximum at the fastest rate among existing regression-based approaches. Applying the method to 174 characteristic-based factors together with the market factor, we obtain an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of 3.59, substantially outperforming competing strategies and delivering the smallest aggregate pricing errors. The selected factors vary over time in both composition and number, averaging about 50. We further develop a model comparison test and reject the hypothesis that eight widely used sparse factor models are sufficient to span the pricing kernel. This paper was accepted by Kay Giesecke, finance. title: From Employer Responsibility to Environmental Irresponsibility: Unintended Impacts of Social Insurance Law on Pollution Emissions
authors: Yanan Li; Yu Qin; Wenjun Wang
affiliations: Business School, Beijing Normal University, Beijing 100875, China; Department of Applied Economics, Guanghua School of Management, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China; Carbon Neutrality and Climate Change Thrust, Society Hub, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Guangzhou 511453, China
abstract: This study investigates the unintended effect of the introduction of the 2011 Social Insurance Law on corporate pollution emissions. Using a difference-in-differences framework, our analysis reveals that enhanced social insurance contributions lead to higher industrial pollution emissions, as measured by chemical oxygen demand and wastewater emissions. The mechanism analysis indicates that the enforcement of the law increases firms’ labor costs and financial distress, motivating them to reduce efforts on end-of-pipe treatment activities and measures taken during the production process, which results in higher pollution emission intensity. Our study highlights the potential conflict between employee protection and corporate environmental goals. Further analysis suggests that stronger environmental monitoring and environmental, social, and governance disclosure requirements can partially mitigate this tradeoff, providing valuable insights for policymakers. This paper was accepted by Caroline Flammer, sustainability. Funding: Y. Li acknowledges research support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72403026]. Y. title: Robust Auction Design with Support Information
authors: Jerry Anunrojwong; Santiago R. Balseiro; Omar Besbes
affiliations: Yale School of Management, New Haven, Connecticut 06511; Graduate School of Business, Columbia University, New York, New York 10027
abstract: A seller wants to sell an item to n buyers. Buyer valuations are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) according to a distribution unknown to the seller; the seller only knows that the support is included in [a, b]. To be robust, the seller chooses a dominant strategy incentive compatible mechanism that optimizes the worst-case performance relative to the ideal expected revenue the seller could have collected with knowledge of buyers’ valuations. Our analysis unifies the regret and the ratio objectives. For these objectives, we derive an optimal mechanism and the corresponding performance in quasi-closed form, as a function of the support information [a, b] and the number of buyers n. Our analysis reveals three regimes of support information and a new class of robust mechanisms. (i) When a/b is below a threshold, the optimal mechanism is a second-price auction (SPA) with random reserve, a focal class in earlier literature. (ii) When a/b is above another threshold, SPAs are strictly suboptimal, and an optimal mechanism belongs to a class of mechanisms we introduce, which we call pooling auctions (POOL); whenever the highest value is above a threshold, the mechanism still allocates to the highest bidder, but otherwise the mechanism allocates to a uniformly random buyer, that is, pools low types. (iii) When a/b is between two thresholds, a randomization between SPA and POOL is optimal. We also characterize optimal mechanisms within nested central subclasses of mechanisms: standard mechanisms that only allocate to the highest bidder, SPA with random reserve, and SPA with no reserve. We show strict separations in terms of performance across classes, implying that deviating from standard mechanisms is necessary for robustness. Lastly, we show that the same results hold under other distribution classes that capture “positive dependence,” namely i.i.d., mixture of i.i.d., and exchangeable and affiliated distributions, as well as i.i.d. regular distributions. This paper was accepted by David Simchi-Levi, revenue management and market analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendices are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.02703 .

title: Building Digital Resilience against Major Shocks
authors: Waifong Boh; Panos Constantinides; Balaji Padmanabhan; Siva Viswanathan
affiliations: Nanyang Technological University; University of Manchester; University of South Florida; University of Maryland
abstract: Major shocks such as the COVID-19 pandemic create unique and exceptional challenges for different entities, including individuals, groups, and organizations. In this special issue editorial, we introduce the concept of digital resilience, which refers to the capabilities developed through the use of digital technologies to absorb major shocks, adapt to disruptions caused by the shocks, and transform to a new stable state, where entities are more prepared to deal with major shocks. The individual papers in this special issue offer compelling examples of how digital resilience is exhibited and how the process of digital resilience can unfold in response to specific major shocks. Drawing upon and extending these papers, we present an integrated framework of how digital technology can help build resilience capabilities, which is missing in past research but needed to mitigate and manage future major shocks, including financial recessions and climate change. We conclude with four important themes for future IS research.

title: Bots with Empathy: Reactance Against Emotion-Aware AI Agents in Customer Service
authors: Elizabeth Han; Dezhi Yin; Han Zhang
affiliations: McGill University; University of South Florida; Hong Kong Baptist University
abstract: The advance of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies has enabled chatbots to be emotionally responsive. In customer service, expressing empathy is a critical component of employee emotional responsiveness and a popular recovery strategy following service failure. However, the impact of empathy expressed by a chatbot is less clear. In this research, we investigate how and why chatbot-expressed empathy after service failure may influence customers’ service evaluations differently. Extending the psychological reactance literature, we propose that an empathetic chatbot may trigger customer reactance due to the unique nature of AI chatbots (vs. humans). We further propose that the triggered reactance can undermine perceptions of a chatbot’s competence and warmth, ultimately hurting service evaluations. We conducted three laboratory experiments to test these predictions. Our theoretical framework and findings illuminate the more nuanced and distinct role of empathy expressed by AI chatbots, and they suggest a critical need for chatbot developers and companies deploying chatbots to be aware of user reactance in customer service.

title: Winning at Defense by Playing Offense: Discrediting by Target Firms in Activist Hedge Fund Campaigns
authors: Matthias Brauer; Marc J. Mertens; Louis Vandepoele
affiliations: University of Mannheim; Copenhagen Business School
abstract: Prior research highlights the far-reaching strategic and governance consequences for firms targeted in activist hedge fund (AHF) campaigns. Yet, how target firm executives and directors can effectively defend against these campaigns remains underexplored. Drawing on impression management (IM) theory, we reason that executives and directors use discrediting in their public rebuttal letters to negatively influence shareholders’ evaluations of AHFs’ reputation. To nuance this prediction, we develop a taxonomy distinguishing between source-focused discrediting, which directly attacks AHFs’ reputation, and message-focused discrediting, which challenges the validity of AHFs’ claims to indirectly tarnish their reputation. We theorize that both discrediting subtypes enhance target firms’ defense success, particularly when deployed in combination. Adopting a temporal perspective on IM theory, we further argue that the effectiveness of discrediting diminishes as more time elapses between an AHF’s public attack and executives and directors’ rebuttal. A manual content analysis of 841 rebuttal letters issued during U.S. AHF campaigns (2000–2023) provides robust support for these predictions. Beyond contributing to shareholder activism research by offering new insights into the determinants of campaign outcomes, our study advances IM theory by conceptualizing discrediting as a multidimensional influence tactic and exploring its effectiveness and temporal dynamics in adversarial contexts.

title: Protestantism and insurance—an elective affinity? A multilevel comparative-historical analysis of the confessional insurance gap
authors: Sebastian Kohl
affiliations: Department of Sociology, Free University Berlin , Berlin 14195,
abstract: Abstract While there are many studies and theories about the rise of social insurance and the public welfare state, the prior emergence and growth of private life and nonlife insurance are largely understudied, mostly due to a lack of data. This article fills this gap by testing whether there is an elective affinity between the rise and evolution of private insurance and Protestantism that is irreducible to typical factors external to religion (gross domestic product, education, demography, public welfare). Drawing on multiple new datasets, the paper tests whether Catholic–Protestant differences in insurance demand persist when controlling for standard covariates external to religion across nineteen OECD countries (1870–2020), across states in the confessionally mixed federations of Germany, Switzerland and the USA (1876–2020) as well as across US counties and European cities around 1909. The article finds Lutheran and Reformed Protestant areas to have had higher private insurance penetration and density than Catholic ones, controlling for standard covariates. This relationship is more pronounced in life than nonlife branches, more pronounced for insurance demand than insurance company activity, and more consistently found in Europe than within the USA. More generally, the article suggests that the confessional insurance gap may provide a missing empirical link to better understand the emergence of Alpine and Maritime insurance cultures, different premodern poor-ethics traditions and the different worlds of modern welfare states and pension systems.

title: Racial pain, academic profit: Methodological reparations for race research under whiteness
authors: Fatima Khan
affiliations: School of Sociology and Criminology, Manchester Metropolitan University, UK
abstract: This article examines how whiteness (as epistemology and as property) structures marketised, racially stratified universities, generating ethical and methodological contradictions in white-led research on race-stratified issues. Ethically, it theorises a structural racial conflict of interest: scholars insulated from racial harm are positioned by whiteness to lead research on race-stratified issues beyond the academy and convert its products into academic profit. Methodologically, it argues that whiteness in white-led qualitative race research collapses credibility at the points of elicitation and recognition, rendering canonical standards of rigour structurally unattainable. As reparation for these conditions, the article introduces Critical Race Participatory Research (CRPR) organised around four auditable commitments: racial-colonial literacy, reflexivity on interest convergence, de-fetishising impact, and participation as praxis, not profit. It repurposes governance mechanisms to redistribute power, enforce accountability, and counter racial extractivism. Although grounded in the UK, the analysis and CRPR commitments travel across Global North research economies wherever whiteness structures research leadership.

title: Information Spillovers Across Media Markets: Risk Perceptions and Cyclospora Outbreaks in U.S. Bagged Salads
authors: Xuerui Yang; Andrew S. Hanks; Robert L. Scharff
affiliations: Department of Family Youth and Community Sciences, University of Florida, Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences; Department of Human Sciences The Ohio State University
abstract: ABSTRACT From 2018 to 2022, contamination of fresh produce by Cyclospora cayetanensis , primarily affecting bagged salads, caused more than 3,300 outbreak‐associated illnesses across the United States. Yet the economic consequences of these outbreaks, and the role of information exposure in shaping consumer responses, remain poorly understood. This study quantifies changes in bagged salad purchases and associated retail losses during six selected large multistate outbreaks occurring from 2018 to 2022 and examines how risk perceptions evolve across outbreak‐affected and neighboring regions. Guided by a risk perception framework emphasizing risk proximity and information‐driven belief updating, we integrate epidemiologic outbreak data, designated market area (DMA)‐level Google Trends search intensity as a geographically granular proxy for information exposure, and NielsenIQ household purchase data. Because DMAs often cross state lines, this design identifies information spillovers to non‐outbreak states sharing a media market. A Heckman selection framework accounts for purchase participation and unobserved heterogeneity, while complementary retail scanner data assess whether retailer stocking adjustments contributed to the observed purchase declines. Across the outbreak periods examined in this study, weekly bagged salad purchases declined by an average of 3.89%, implying cumulative retail losses of approximately $373.67 million. Outbreak‐specific searches (e.g., “Cyclospora”) were associated with greater perceived risk and larger purchase reductions, while general salad‐related searches were associated with smaller reductions. Spillovers across shared media markets further reduced purchases in non‐outbreak states by 3.33% per week. Retailer analysis found no statistically significant store‐level stocking reductions during outbreak or recall periods, supporting the interpretation that the observed purchase declines were primarily demand‐driven. These findings highlight the economic significance of information‐driven consumer responses and the importance of timely, accurate, and geographically targeted risk communication during foodborne outbreaks.

title: Systemic Risk Revisited: A Working Definition and Diagnostic Framework for Risk Analysis
authors: Jianping Yan; Jiahong Wen; Jiquan Zhang; Qinmian Bai
affiliations: Key Laboratory of Resilient Cities and Integrated Risk Management of Shanghai Emergency Management Bureau Shanghai Normal University Shanghai China; Rodel Risk Solutions Inc. Toronto Canada; School of Environment and Geographical Sciences Shanghai Normal University Shanghai China; School of Environment Northeast Normal University Changchun China; Jilin Province Science and Technology Innovation Center of Agro‐Meteorological Disaster Risk Assessment and Prevention Jilin Province Science and Technology Innovation Center of Agro‐Meteorological Disaster Risk Assessment and Prevention Changchun China
abstract: ABSTRACT Systemic risk has gained increasing attention across disaster risk reduction, climate governance, finance, infrastructure, and other domains, yet its meaning and application remain inconsistent. Existing definitions emphasize interdependence, contagion, complexity, uncertainty, cascading effects, and system‐wide disruption, but differ in analytical focus and operational use. This paper reviews major definitional traditions and argues that a working definition and diagnostic framework can clarify the analytical basis of systemic risk. We define systemic risk as potential damage, loss, and impact that propagate through interdependencies, feedbacks, and nonlinear processes within or across interconnected systems. Building on this definition, the paper develops a diagnostic framework based on system structure, propagation pathways, dynamic mechanisms, and cascading consequences. These dimensions help distinguish systemic risks from risks that are severe, complex, or large scale but remain relatively contained, and provide a structured basis for examining how adverse consequences propagate within and across interconnected systems in different domains.

title: An Agent‐Based Model for Post‐Disaster Resource Allocation Considering Dynamic Demand
authors: Xihui Wang; Wanting Shao; Yu Fan; Liang Liang
affiliations: School of Management University of Science and Technology of China Hefei China; Key Laboratory of Emergency Logistics and Relief Supply Provision Ministry of Emergency Management Langfang China; School of Safety Engineering Jiangxi University of Science and Technology Ganzhou China
abstract: ABSTRACT In the response phase of a disaster, effective and equitable resource allocation is critical for meeting the needs of affected populations and maintaining the social order in disaster‐stricken areas. However, dynamic demand driven by the mobility of disaster‐affected populations can substantially impact resource allocation outcomes. To consider this mobility in the resource allocation problem, in this paper, we employ an agent‐based model to simulate cross‐shelter movements and assess the performance of resource allocation strategies considering a gradual increase of total available resources over time. A novel resource allocation strategy is proposed, which leverages demand estimation through a machine learning (ML) method‐XGBoost. We then compare this approach against two conventional strategies: uniform distribution and historical data averaging. Through case studies using real‐world data of Typhoon Ragasa from Shenzhen in China and Lal‐lo in the Philippines, we demonstrate that our proposed strategy comprehensively outperforms the other two in terms of effectiveness, equity and stability. In conclusion, this ML‐based prediction approach offers valuable insights to support decision‐makers in the formulation of resource allocation plans.

title: Assessment of Risks, Efficiency, Costs, and Gain of Natural Hazard (Catastrophe) Consequences Prevention Based on Geophysical Monitoring
authors: Leonid F. Chernogor; Leonid L. Chornohor
affiliations: Department of Space Radio Physics V. N. Karazin Kharkiv National University Kharkiv Ukraine; Laboratory of Environmental Research, State Scientific Institution “Institute for Single Crystals” Kharkiv Ukraine
abstract: ABSTRACT The purpose of this paper is to quantitatively estimate the efficiency of forecasting hazards and catastrophic processes induced by high‐energy terrestrial sources, based on an integrated monitoring of the state of geophysical processes. Using methods of mathematical statistics and detection theory, relations have been obtained that can be used to calculate the coefficients of the efficiency of warning of catastrophes and the costs associated with a predicted event. The hazard (catastrophe) prevention efficiency coefficient has been shown to be dependent only on the conditional probability of missing a hazard. The relative cost parameter is a function of five parameters: a priori probability of the unwanted event, a conditional false alarm probability, a conditional missed detect probability, relative costs in the case of false alarm probability, and costs to minimize consequences of the hazardous event in case it has been accurately forecast. The gain from organizing geophysical monitoring has been estimated for a few dangers and catastrophes of terrestrial nature. The gain has been shown to be significant in many cases. An energy‐based classification of the most important natural sources of hazards and catastrophes, as well as their consequences, is proposed or improved.

title: Forecasting LLM‐Enabled Biorisk and the Efficacy of Safeguards
authors: Bridget Williams; Luca Righetti; Josh Rosenberg; Rebecca Ceppas de Castro; Otto Kuusela; Rhiannon Britt; Emily Soice; Alvaro Morales; Jon Sanders; Seth Donoughe; James Black; Ezra Karger; Philip E. Tetlock
affiliations: Forecasting Research Institute Claymont Delaware United States; Centre for the Governance of AI London United Kingdom; SecureBio Cambridge Massachusetts United States; Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security Baltimore Maryland United States; Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago Chicago Illinois United States; Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania Philadelphia Pennsylvania United States
abstract: ABSTRACT Capabilities of large language models (LLMs) on several biological benchmarks have prompted not only excitement about their usefulness for research but also concern about biosecurity risks. We recruited 46 subject‐matter experts in biology and biosecurity, and 22 generalist forecasters to estimate the risks of growing LLM capabilities. Most respondents expected some hypothetical LLM capabilities to increase their estimates of risk and dramatically underestimated the rate of LLM progress in those capabilities. When these capabilities arose, the median forecast did update as anticipated. The median expert initially predicted a 0.3% annual risk of a human‐caused epidemic that causes 100,000 deaths. This estimate then rose to 1.5% conditional on several hypothetical LLM capabilities, including matching the performance of a top‐performing team of virologists on a virology troubleshooting test, which the median expert did not expect to occur until 2030. Given this finding, we conducted a baselining study and found that LLMs already crossed this performance threshold in April 2025. A follow‐up survey conducted after these results were available found that forecasters significantly updated their median unconditional risk estimates upward, with the new median expert forecast of annual risk rising to 1.5% (as anticipated by the earlier conditional forecasts). More encouragingly, most experts thought that the adoption of LLM safeguards and mandatory nucleic acid screening would negate the risk associated with some hypothetical LLM capabilities.

title: EXPRESS: A Learning and Searching Method for Integrated Process Planning and Scheduling
authors: Hongpei Li; Han Zhang; Ziyan He; Jiaqi Hu; Hongsong Yuan
abstract: The integrated process planning and scheduling problem combines process route planning and shop scheduling to achieve high efficiency in manufacturing and maximize resource utilization, which is crucial for modern manufacturing systems. Traditional approaches, such as mixed-integer linear programming and heuristic algorithms, often struggle to balance solution quality and computational efficiency, particularly in large-scale scenarios. To address this, we propose learning-then-searching, an efficient framework combining deep reinforcement learning with heuristic search to solve integrated process planning and scheduling problems. We formulate the problem as a Markov decision process and develop a deep reinforcement learning method tailored to capture the complex relationships among operations, machines, and jobs. With the learned policy distributions, Monte Carlo tree search employs learned priors and problem-specific rollouts to further refine scheduling strategies, effectively balancing exploration and exploitation to achieve better solutions. Experimental results show that the proposed framework improves solution efficiency and quality over traditional methods across benchmark and large-scale instances, with pronounced advantages when route ambiguity is high. It also offers practitioners a flexible tradeoff between rapid policy-based decisions and further refinement through tree search when additional computation time is available.

title: Shared Policy Commitments in the Buyer Ego‐Network and Buyer Financial Performance: A Multiplex Network Perspective
authors: Jesus Diego; Maria J. Montes‐Sancho; Zhaohui Wu
affiliations: Department of Information Systems, Supply Chain Management & Decision Support NEOMA Business School Reims France; Department of Business Administration Universidad Carlos III de Madrid Madrid Spain; College of Business Oregon State University Corvallis Oregon USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Public commitments to sustainability policies have become common practice among buyer and supplier companies facing growing sustainability imperatives. Firms often pursue these commitments to address societal expectations and comply with institutional norms rather than to achieve efficiency, frequently endorsing them without a comprehensive assessment of their performance implications. Within the supply chain, when multiple firms commit to similar policies, alignment emerges across network members through shared policy commitments. Such shared commitments differ from traditional buyer–supplier coordinated alignment by introducing an additional layer of complexity beyond contractual dynamics, with potential performance consequences. Adopting an embeddedness perspective, the authors analyze 240 multiplex ego networks that capture both shared policy commitments and structural ties. Results show that shared policy commitments within a buyer ego‐network, between a buyer and its direct suppliers or among those suppliers, are positively associated with the focal buyer's financial performance, with each direction's association conditional on the level of the other. However, the findings also reveal a curvilinear relationship: buyer performance declines as network members' commitments become increasingly centered on the same policies. Network interconnectedness through contractual ties serves as a moderator, unlocking additional benefits of shared commitments. This study provides theoretical and practical insights for managing shared commitments in the buyer ego‐network while avoiding over‐embeddedness.

title: Reconfiguring external and internal networks for resilience, agility and ambidexterity under geopolitical volatility
authors: Umair Tanveer; Thinh Gia Hoang; Shamaila Ishaq; Stefan Gold
affiliations: Business School, University of Exeter–Streatham Campus , ,; Ho Chi Minh City University of Economics and Finance(UEF) , ,; Derby International Business School, University of Derby , ,; TUM Campus Straubing for Biotechnology and Sustainability, Technical University of Munich , ,
abstract: Purpose Geopolitical tensions and economic policy volatility are compelling multinational firms to redesign both external supply chain networks and their intra-organisational networks of plants, subsidiaries and governance. This study examines how intra-organisational networks are redesigned in response to geopolitically induced reshaping of external supply chain networks and how this redesign enables resilience, agility and ambidexterity. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a qualitative multiple-case design with three longitudinal focal cases and five supporting cases. The data comprise 58 semi-structured interviews, supplemented by secondary documents to reconstruct case trajectories over time. Findings Geopolitically driven external network reshaping heightens dependence and power asymmetry through concentrated bottlenecks, low substitutability, and compliance-gated access. Firms respond through buffering, bridging, and selective internalisation, but these moves become effective only when internal decision rights, subsidiary mandates, and integration capacity are redesigned. Originality/value The study conceptualises external and intra-organisational network restructuring as a coupled, dependence-driven process under geopolitical volatility. It extends Resource Dependence Theory by showing that dependence-management strategies require internal re-architecture to become executable, thereby reframing resilience, agility, and ambidexterity as outcomes of organisational redesign rather than static capabilities.

title: The Role of Institutions in the Relationship Between Informal Competition and New Product Development in Emerging Economies
authors: Sadrac Cenophat; Martin Eisend
affiliations: EM Strasbourg Business School Université de Strasbourg Strasbourg France; The University of Vienna Wien Austria
abstract: ABSTRACT Academic Summary Research has argued that informal competition (IC)—the competitive pressure from firms that are unregistered but derive income from the production of legal goods and services—increases formal (i.e., legally registered) firms' engagement in new product development (NPD) in emerging economies. However, other studies have suggested that IC may decrease such engagement. Drawing on an institutional perspective, we argue that the relationship between IC and NPD is contingent on the level of IC and the influence of formal and informal institutions. A multilevel analysis of 29,520 formal firms across 21 emerging economies indicates an inverted U‐shaped relationship between IC and NPD probability. Low to moderate levels of IC increase NPD probability, whereas higher levels reduce it. The findings also reveal that this relationship varies across emerging economies, with significant cross‐level interactions between IC and elements of formal (e.g., regulatory control, availability of finance) and informal institutions (e.g., survival vs. self‐expression and traditional vs. secular‐rational values) shaping NPD probability. Managerial Summary Informal competition can stimulate formal firms' new product development at low to moderate levels, but high levels of IC can discourage it. Because informal firms spur innovation among their formal counterparts, policymakers should not automatically seek to eliminate IC. Instead, they should consider IC as a changing condition and adapt enforcement to its intensity. At low to moderate levels of IC, minimal enforcement may be appropriate as the innovation and consumer benefits associated with IC may outweigh its costs. As IC becomes more intense and begins to undermine formal firms' NPD, policymakers can tighten enforcement while offering informal firms incentives to formalize. For managers, the findings suggest that the strategic response to IC should also depend on its intensity. When IC is low, formal firms may continue to innovate despite financial constraints; managers can therefore pursue low‐risk, affordable products using frugal innovation methods, while policymakers can support these efforts through improved access to finance. Managers are also well‐advised to consider the institutional context. Unlike their counterparts in countries leaning toward survival values (e.g., India), formal firms operating in societies that lean toward self‐expression values (e.g., Uruguay) are more likely to engage in NPD when IC is low; the probability decreases as IC becomes higher.

title: HOW AND WHY CHANGE AGENTS LEVERAGE AMBIGUITY: DIGITAL CHANGE AS A PROGRESSION OF PROCESS CONFIGURATIONS
authors: Jonny Holmstrom; Kalle Lyytinen; Daniel Nylen; Viktor Arvidsson
affiliations: Umea Universitet; Case Western Reserve University; Linköping University
abstract: Digital change (DC) broadly entails a radical reconfiguration of an organization’s modus operandi through the deployment of a growing and often untried set of digital technologies. Prior research has extensively examined DC in terms of outcomes, antecedents, and mechanisms. However, one critical aspect remains underexplored: the role of ambiguity arising from unknown technologies, non-linear change processes, and the coexistence of multiple organizational goals. Existing DC literature commonly attributes failure to an inability to remove ambiguity – that is, the contested and fluid meanings, goals, and means of DC – and to align clear strategic intent with well-defined technology functions. We challenge this view by conceptualizing ambiguity not as a problem to be eliminated, but as an inherent and generative condition of DC that must be actively reckoned with. Drawing on March’s distinction between goal ambiguity and technology ambiguity, we develop a framework of four DC configurations based on the presence or absence of ambiguity in strategic intent and in the articulated role of digital technologies. We analyze four DC cases, treating each as a progression through shifting configurations of goal and technology ambiguity. Using three longitudinal empirical cases and one baseline alignment case from prior literature, we identify four distinct DC pathways, each characterized by a specific sequence of configurations. We theorize how ambiguity shapes DC trajectories and outcomes and show that practitioners may need to deliberately increase or decrease ambiguity in goals and/or technology functions to propel DC forward.

title: From Gender Antagonism to Inclusive Solidarity? Trade Union Membership and Attitudes Toward Women's Employment
authors: Jianxuan Lei
affiliations: Department of Work and Organizations, Carlson School of Management University of Minnesota Minneapolis Minnesota USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Why and to what extent do union members differ from non‐members in attitudes toward women's employment? This study argues that a masculinized conception of work has historically underpinned gender antagonism in trade unionism, and that the rise of right‐wing populism may have hindered recent progress toward gender equality among union members. Analyzing the European Values Study data, I find that union members hold more egalitarian attitudes toward women's employment than non‐members on average. This relationship further varies across individual and institutional characteristics. After the financial crisis, however, the positive association has weakened particularly in countries where right‐wing populism is influential.

title: Responsible Management Education and Its Potential as an Epistemic Object of Change
authors: Valtteri A. Aaltonen; Marjo E. Siltaoja
affiliations: Department of Environmental Sciences, Faculty of Biological and Environmental Sciences University of Helsinki Helsinki Finland; Management and Leadership Jyväskylä University School of Business and Economics Jyväskylä Finland
abstract: Abstract This study examines whether and how RME can be performed as an epistemic object to broaden business schools’ education on climate change. The research builds on a qualitative case study involving 10 Finnish business schools. The analysis reveals that RME is performed as both an epistemic object and a boundary object, with different implications for its embeddedness within institutions. Our findings show how accreditations have introduced RME as a boundary object enforcing performativity around sustainability themes yet enabling disciplines to maintain their distinct or limited roles. At the same time, RME is met with both resistance and compliance, depending on how well the object fits with disciplinary boundaries and career trajectories. Lastly, as an epistemic object, RME encourages co‐reflexivity, which is essential for climate‐proofing business schools. We discuss the possibilities of a hybrid orientation of RME as both a boundary object and an epistemic object for enforcing climate‐orientation in management education.

title: Harnessing Power Through External Collaborative Innovation: How Incumbent Inventors Navigate Rising Talent Influx in Developed‐country MNE Subsidiaries
authors: Tianjiao Xia; Xiaohui Liu
affiliations: Norwich Business School University of East Anglia Norwich UK; Birmingham Business School University of Birmingham Birmingham UK
abstract: Abstract This paper examines how, and under what conditions, the increasing presence of highly skilled local employees (HSLEs) within subsidiaries of developed‐country multinational enterprises (DCMNEs) influences incumbent local inventors’ external collaborative innovation. Adopting a power dependence perspective, we propose that incumbent local inventors are more likely to engage in external than internal collaborative innovation in response to the increasing presence of HSLEs. Successful external collaborative innovation enhances incumbent local inventors’ bargaining power by enabling them to gain stronger positions within external networks critical to DCMNEs’ innovation and to access alternative employment opportunities. We further contend that the positive relationship between the increasing presence of HSLEs and incumbent local inventors’ external collaborative innovation is strengthened by the boundary‐spanning characteristics of the management hierarchies, such as cross‐cultural CEOs and interlocking directors. Our analysis of DCMNE subsidiaries operating in China provides empirical support for these predictions. This research offers novel and important insights into collaborating‐by‐hiring, highlighting the increasing presence of HSLEs as a competitive mechanism for interorganizational collaborative innovation and emphasizing the strategic importance of externally leveraging the knowledge and expertise of incumbent inventors.

title: How Assumptions About Time Divide and Connect Epistemic Communities in Business and Management
authors: Stephanie Decker
affiliations: University of Birmingham Birmingham UK
abstract: Abstract Business and management studies comprise distinct epistemic communities that frequently do not interact or collaborate. While this has been explained as paradigm incommensurability, construct ambiguity or the variance–process, this CrossRoads article sets out a less commonly invoked source of difference: how our theories conceptualize time. This includes assumptions about whether the future is determined or open (temporal openness), whether and how change takes place (temporal directionality) and the appropriate timescales and detail for analysis (temporal duration). To illustrate the importance of these three temporal dimensions, influential traditions in strategy, entrepreneurship, institutional theory, process studies, population ecology, real‐options and scenario planning are mapped. The mapping demonstrates that many temporal differences between epistemic communities are differences of degree that may offer productive tensions for collaborative approaches, even though some may remain difficult to reconcile. Through a set of diagnostic questions, this CrossRoads piece offers a framework for interdisciplinary temporal brokerage within and beyond business and management.

title: Digitalization and Cybersecurity: Firm‐level Evidence
authors: Jukka Sihvonen
affiliations: University of Vaasa Vaasa Finland
abstract: Abstract Digitalization has opposing effects on cybersecurity: While new digital technologies can strengthen security capabilities, they simultaneously expand potential attack surfaces. To determine which effect dominates, we analyse 9606 US firm‐years (2006–2023) with 543 documented breaches and find that increased digitalization, measured through 10‐K business descriptions, significantly raises the likelihood of future cyber breaches. A one‐standard‐deviation increase in digitalization corresponds to up to a 10 percentage point higher breach probability, driven primarily by organizational rather than technological dimensions. Expert auditors and cybersecurity disclosure reduce breach likelihood, but their protective effect attenuates as digitalization rises; that of board and C‐suite technology expertise instead strengthens. These findings qualify the protective role of conventional monitoring in highly digitalized firms and point to a repositioning of cybersecurity governance from external monitoring towards digital expertise embedded in strategic decision‐making.

title: Unmanagement Education for the Age of Climate Crisis
authors: Fernanda Cassab Carreira; Isleide Arruda Fontenelle
affiliations: FGV EAESP Av. Nove de Julho, 2029, Bela Vista São Paulo 01313–902 Brazil
abstract: Abstract This paper examines how embodied, situated and relational experiences outside‐the‐classroom can open space for epistemic dislocations in Management Education under conditions of ecological crisis. Drawing on a qualitative pedagogical experience in a sustainability course in Brazil, informed by Design‐Based Research—whose assumptions of control, design and predictability we critically question–we explore conditions under which radical imaginaries may emerge through such experiences. Students engaged in encounters with human and non‐human others that generated discomfort and tension with habitual ways of knowing, opening possibilities for the emergence of (dis)enchanted imaginaries of Nature and (de)colonial imaginaries. These dynamics were intensified through situated and embodiment engagements, which at times gave rise to epistemic dislocations, or moments in which established ways of knowing lose their capacity to organize experience as alternative imaginaries become available. Those dislocations created temporary openings for participants to re‐examine their understandings of Nature, coloniality and socio‐ecological relations, remaining susceptible to reabsorption into dominant managerial frames. We contribute to climate‐oriented pedagogy by introducing Unmanagement Education, a reflexive pedagogical approach grounded in non‐mastery, embodiment and situated relationality, that may unsettle instituted imaginaries, opening space for epistemic dislocations to emerge under conditions of ecological crisis.

title: Asset Market Participation, Redistribution, and Asset Pricing
authors: Francesco Saverio Gaudio; Ivan Petrella; Emiliano Santoro
affiliations: Sapienza University of Rome Rome Italy; Collegio Carlo Alberto and University of Turin Turin Italy; CEPR London UK; Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore Milan Italy
abstract: ABSTRACT We study how redistribution between asset holders and non‐asset holders links macroeconomic fluctuations to expected stock returns. Aggregate and relative consumption growth forecast excess returns with opposite signs and at different horizons. We interpret these patterns using a production‐based asset‐pricing model with limited participation and external habits. Aggregate (relative) consumption captures variation in the price (quantity) of risk. Technology shocks drive macroeconomic fluctuations, whereas redistributive shocks generate large short‐run movements in inequality and are the main source of priced risk. This points to a macro‐finance disconnect between the drivers of business cycles and those governing risk premia.

title: Real Activity and Uncertainty Shocks: The Long and the Short of It
authors: Mathias Krogh; Giovanni Pellegrino
affiliations: Jyske Bank and Department of Economics and Business Economics Aarhus University Aarhus Denmark; Department of Economics and Management University of Padova Padova Italy
abstract: ABSTRACT We propose a nonrecursive VAR identification strategy that separately identifies short‐term and long‐term uncertainty shocks by exploiting sign restrictions implied by a stylized framework and a DSGE model featuring both types of shocks. We find that long‐term uncertainty shocks exert strong and persistent effects on real activity, whereas short‐term shocks have limited real effects. We use the DSGE model to study their differential propagation and show that time‐to‐build is an important ingredient allowing the model to account for the stark empirical asymmetry in investment and, in turn, output—both contract sharply after long‐term shocks but only modestly after short‐term shocks.

title: Union Membership and Native-Immigrant Labour Market Gaps
authors: Samuel Dodini; Alexander Willén; Julia Li Zhu
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas; Norwegian School of Economics Department of Economics,; San Diego State University Department of Economics,
abstract: Abstract We estimate the causal effects of union membership on labour market outcomes for natives and immigrants, exploiting quasi-experimental variation from large increases in Norway’s tax deduction for union dues. Union membership raises earnings and improves employment protection for native workers, while the private returns for non-Western immigrants are substantially smaller and often close to zero. Complementary survey evidence suggests that this gap is not explained by differences in information, preferences, or engagement with unions: immigrants receive similar information when joining, report similar preferences over job amenities, and are more likely than natives to seek union assistance. Instead, the combined administrative and survey evidence is consistent with differences in union-side behaviour. Immigrants report lower satisfaction after contacting unions for support and are more likely to believe that native workers and those with strong local networks receive greater benefits from membership. The impact is most pronounced in concentrated labour markets, indicating that relying on unions to address monopsony-based market failures may unintentionally amplify group inequalities.

title: State Ownership and the History of Capitalism
authors: Aldo Musacchio
affiliations: Brandeis University and NBER
abstract: Abstract Dominant narratives in economics and the history of capitalism treat state ownership and state capitalism as deviations from privately organized market capitalism. This article synthesizes historical scholarship to explain how public enterprises became permanent features of capitalism by addressing persistent failures in capital markets, infrastructure provision, and industrial coordination. It traces four stages, from nineteenth-century network integration and wartime entrepreneurship to postwar industrial ecosystem building and the reinvention of state ownership through privatization and governance reform. This perspective explains resilience through both enduring coordination problems and accumulated organizational capabilities. The article also extends the history of managerial capitalism by showing how state-owned enterprises fostered professional management, technical expertise, and internal labor markets, often before comparable private firms emerged. Especially in late-industrializing economies, public enterprises helped build the organizational foundations of private-sector development. State ownership thus emerges as an enduring organizational form through which capitalism itself developed and evolved.

title: Shaken and Stirred: Martini & Rossi and the Cycles of Globalization
authors: Sophus A. Reinert; Lorena Barale
affiliations: Harvard Business School; Archivist and Independent Scholar
abstract: Abstract This article draws from Martini & Rossi’s archives to trace the company’s history from its beginnings in Piedmont, Italy, in the mid-nineteenth century to its global expansion in the twentieth century. Martini & Rossi shaped cocktail culture globally, and its history sheds light on how entrepreneurs and firms prospered through cycles of globalization and deglobalization. Just as skilled management and new technologies facilitated vermouth production at home, innovations in salesmanship allowed the company to penetrate new markets abroad. The article highlights how Martini & Rossi emerged as a pioneering multinational and created one of the first global alcohol brands during the first era of global capitalism. It also examines the strategies firms could adopt amid increasing protectionism following the onset of the Great War in 1914, adding nuance to our understanding of how macroeconomic processes of globalization and deglobalization are experienced and navigated by individual companies.

Do Experimental Asset Market Results Replicate? High‐Powered Preregistered Replications of 17 Key Results
authors: CHRISTOPH HUBER; FELIX HOLZMEISTER; MAGNUS JOHANNESSON; CHRISTIAN KÖNIG‐KERSTING; ANNA DREBER; JÜRGEN HUBER; MICHAEL KIRCHLER
abstract: ABSTRACT Experimental asset markets provide a controlled approach to studying financial markets. We attempt to replicate 17 key results from four prominent studies, collecting new data from 166 markets with 1,544 participants. Only three of the 14 original results reported as statistically significant were successfully replicated. We fail to replicate findings on emotions, self‐control, and gender differences in bubble formation but confirm that experience reduces bubbles and cognitive skills explain trading success. Our study demonstrates the importance of replications in enhancing the credibility of scientific results in this field.

title: Correlated Demand Shocks and Asset Pricing
authors: Byungwook Kim
affiliations: University of California , Irvine,
abstract: Abstract I propose a mechanism through which institutional investors’ correlated demand shocks provide a source of market risk in asset pricing. Institutional investors have mandates to beat a similar market index. During periods of strong stock market performance, their incentive to outperform intensifies as more of them fall short of the market index. This incentive induces procyclical risk-taking behavior, generating correlated demand that elevates the market betas and risk premia of exposed stocks. Quasi-experiments using exogenous changes in index membership support a causal interpretation of the mechanism. Elevated betas are associated with a higher perceived cost of capital and reduced firm investment. (JEL G1, G2)

title: Sales-Based CEO Incentives and Their Effect Across the Supply Chain
authors: Jen Choi
affiliations: Korea University Business School
abstract: ABSTRACT I examine how the use of sales performance measures in CEO incentive contracts affects the operations of a firm and its suppliers. A growing number of firms are evaluating and compensating their CEOs based on sales performance. However, because sales performance measures are narrow measures that do not incentivize cost control, they can influence operational decisions that affect not only the firm but also its suppliers. I show that the use of sales performance measures in CEO bonus contracts is associated with inventory fluctuations that increase the bullwhip effect, a phenomenon in which a firm exhibits greater volatility in production than in demand, thereby increasing the order volatility faced by its suppliers. Instrumental variable tests using the firm’s network connections through compensation consultants mitigate concerns that the results are driven by omitted factors. Collectively, my findings illuminate spillover effects of CEO incentive contracts on economically linked firms. Data Availability: Data are available from the sources cited in the text. title: Audit Quality and Audit Partner Ownership of Non-Audit Businesses: Evidence from China
authors: Clive S. Lennox; Zanyue Qi; Xi Wu
affiliations: University of Southern California; Central University of Finance and Economics
abstract: ABSTRACT We examine whether audit partners’ ownership stakes in affiliated non-audit businesses are related to audit quality. We argue that non-audit ownership is a relatively sharp measure of auditor-client economic bonding, which can impair auditor independence. Using a unique setting in China where we observe partners’ equity stakes in both audit and non-audit businesses, we find that audit adjustments are significantly smaller when engagement partners hold larger ownership stakes in non-audit businesses. Audit adjustments are further reduced when the entire audit partnership holds greater ownership in affiliated non-audit businesses, suggesting that non-audit ownership matters at the audit firm level as well. Additional analyses suggest that these results are driven by impaired independence, rather than partner distraction or endogenous partner-client matching. Our study informs ongoing policy debates on the structuring of audit and non-audit businesses as well as the investments of non-audit entities in accounting practices. Data Availability: The authors have nondisclosure and confidentiality agreements for their use of proprietary data, which were provided to the authors for independent academic research only. Nonproprietary data are available from sources identified in the text. JEL Classifications: M41; M42; M48; M52.

title: Analysts’ Perspectives on Climate Change: An Examination of Analyst Reports
authors: Jesse Chan
affiliations: Boston University
abstract: ABSTRACT I explore the nature of analysts’ climate-related discussion in their reports. Focusing on industries most exposed to climate change, I find very few reports (less than 2 percent) and a minority of analysts (less than 11 percent) discuss climate-related topics. Analysts concentrate climate-related discussion among utilities, mostly discussing renewable energy and regulatory issues. These discussions exhibit no significant association with short-term earnings forecasts and a weak association with more pessimistic long-term growth forecast revisions. Climate-related discussion is also associated with more optimistic target prices when analysts do not issue long-term growth forecasts, suggesting the development of a long-term perspective correlates with views on climate-related issues. Discussions of solar-, emissions-, and automotive-related topics are associated with this greater target price optimism. These findings highlight how analysts’ climate-related discussion relates to long-term expectations and concentrates among highly exposed firms. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text. A detailed listing of how each large language model (LLM) classified each climate-related report, a document describing the details of this listing, a firm-year summary of climate-related discussion and subtopical classifications, and a description document of this firm-year summary are available upon request. title: Beyond economic bargaining power? Work-related internal migration and subjective well-being in couples
authors: Elias Hofmann; Nico Stawarz; Nicolai Netz; Heiko Rüger
affiliations: Federal Institute for Population Research (BiB) , Wiesbaden ,; University of Hamburg (UHH) , Hamburg ,; German Centre for Higher Education Research and Science Studies (DZHW) , Hannover ,; Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU) , Mainz ,
abstract: Abstract Bargaining theory posits that both partners’ utility shapes couples’ migration decisions. Yet, most empirical tests focus on individual incomes, thus overlooking non-economic factors in couples’ deliberations about spatial mobility. We argue that considering holistic indicators of utility, such as subjective well-being, can advance our understanding of couples’ decision-making. Using data from the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP, 1991–2021) and fixed effects panel regressions, we analyze changes in life satisfaction following work-related internal migration on both individual and dyadic levels. Moreover, we examine whether these changes depend on shifts in partners’ economic bargaining power (EBP, defined as female partners’ share of total household labor income), thereby evaluating the common assumption that couples’ bargaining centers around income. Our results show that, on average, both partners experience increases in their life satisfaction following migration. Distinguishing whether women’s EBP remains unchanged, decreases, or increases with migration, we find that women’s life satisfaction gains are only weakly related to changes in their EBP. In contrast, men’s life satisfaction only increases if their partner’s EBP decreases or remains unchanged, but not if it increases—a pattern consistent with the notion of gendered expectations about the within-couple income distribution hampering men’s well-being gains. Overall, our findings suggest that well-being is an important factor in couples’ migration decision-making and that income-based measures of bargaining power provide only an incomplete account of partners’ bargaining positions.

title: Economic Self-Interest and Support for Redistribution: New Evidence Using Election Results Data
authors: JIEUN LEE; E. GRANT BALDWIN; G. AGUSTIN MARKARIAN; BENJAMIN J. NEWMAN
affiliations: University of California, Riverside; University of California, Los Angeles; Loyola University Chicago
abstract: A formidable corpus of scholarship explores the role of economic self-interest in shaping public support for redistribution. One striking feature of this literature is its near-exclusive reliance on reported preferences in surveys, with little-to-no research analyzing revealed preferences in the form of actual voting on redistribution. Leveraging eight redistributive ballot initiatives across six American states and a total of 73,053 observations of revealed support for redistribution, we uncover consistent evidence that the economic standing of precinct voters is systematically related to their support for redistribution. We find that lower- to upper-middle-income precincts are each significantly more supportive of redistribution than upper-income precincts, with pronounced decreases in support associated with the increasing prevalence of high-income households subject to proposed tax increases. Finally, we observe the largest class differential in support for redistribution in more heavily Republican precincts.

Globalization and the Hinterland: International Trade and the Rural–Urban Divide
authors: EDWARD D. MANSFIELD; OMER SOLODOCH
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania; Hebrew University of Jerusalem
abstract: The growing political divide between rural and urban regions is often attributed to rural deindustrialization and import competition in manufacturing. Yet this cleavage emerged in many countries well before rural industrialization, pointing to underlying economic forces that existing accounts have overlooked. We argue that comparative advantage in agriculture is one such force: rural voters are more likely to support protectionist parties and policies when local agriculture is uncompetitive, since this sector is often central to their communities’ economic and social life. Using a new harmonized dataset of surveys from 123 countries and extensive data on voting behavior in the European Union, we find strong support for our argument. An additional analysis exploiting exogenous subnational variation in agricultural competitiveness in the United States post-NAFTA further corroborates our findings: the political divide between rural and urban voters is pronounced in uncompetitive regions but negligible in those possessing a comparative advantage in agriculture.

title: When Firms Lead States: Financial Intermediaries and the Politics of Sovereign Green Bond Issuance
authors: Monica Widmann
affiliations: Seton Hall University
abstract: Abstract Sovereign green bonds typically appear only after corporate green bond issuance has accumulated—a sequence at odds with the policy consensus that sovereign borrowing anchors debt market development. I argue that the inversion reflects market building by global investment banks. The four banks that authored the Green Bond Principles in 2014 used early private corporate transactions to build the verification practices, pricing conventions, and investor networks needed for a functioning market, then served as lead managers when sovereigns entered, transferring accumulated expertise across the public–private divide. States entered a market whose institutional infrastructure they did not design. The Cox proportional hazards model shows that accumulated corporate issuance significantly accelerates sovereign entry, while government agency issuance delays it by substituting for direct sovereign participation. A bank-level triangulation shows that founding-bank presence at sovereign entry reflects green-bond-specific expertise transfer rather than general dominance in sovereign debt underwriting. The findings identify financial intermediaries as a distinct channel through which sustainable finance reaches sovereign borrowers and show how privately constructed market conditions shape the terms on which states engage with global climate finance.
